title: Keir Starmer Leaves Downing Street as Andy Burnham Becomes Britain's New PM
excerpt: The outgoing PM departed with an emotional farewell after two turbulent years, leaving behind a complicated legacy with Britain's Indian community — from his love of Indian cuisine to the Diwali controversy.
body:
• Keir Starmer formally resigned as UK Prime Minister on Monday, with Andy Burnham becoming Britain's fourth PM in four years after receiving an invitation from King Charles to form a government.
  • Starmer's relationship with the British Indian community was marked by both warmth — including a celebrated visit to Mumbai's Khyber restaurant — and missteps, most notably the Diwali controversy at Downing Street.
  • Burnham has pledged cost-of-living relief "starting tomorrow" and a ten-year plan for Britain, while hospitality industry bodies hope for reduced business rates and VAT cuts.

A Tearful Exit from Number 10

Sir Keir Starmer left 10 Downing Street on Monday with a farewell speech that combined stoicism with visible emotion. Flanked by his wife Victoria and closest supporters — cabinet ministers Rachel Reeves, David Lammy, Steve Reed, and London Mayor Sadiq Khan among them — the outgoing PM thanked the British people for the opportunity to serve.

"For all the focus on individuals, politics is a team sport," Starmer said outside Number 10. "I go with good grace, I go with a smile, and I go proud of everything we have achieved." He added that immigration was down significantly and the country was more secure and prosperous than when he took office.

The more emotional side of the departure had already played out. When Starmer announced his resignation on June 22, his speech cracked as he paid tribute to his wife for being "by my side through good times and bad" and broke down entirely when he spoke of his "beautiful children" and promised to be "the best dad I can."

"Every decision I've taken has been about putting the country I love first. I will support my successor and do everything I can to ensure an orderly handover of power."

— Keir Starmer, resignation speech

A Complicated Legacy with British Indians

Starmer's relationship with Britain's Indian community was a study in contrasts. On one hand, his genuine appreciation for Indian culture and cuisine was well-documented. During a two-day visit to India in October 2025, Starmer hosted a 40-person dinner at Mumbai's iconic Khyber restaurant, the 65-year-old Kala Ghoda institution renowned for its North-West Frontier cuisine. Earlier, he had featured Mr Singh's Indian Restaurant from Glasgow at a St Andrew's Day celebration at Downing Street, making tandoori salmon tikka — the restaurant's signature dish — a talking point of the evening.

On the other hand, his Downing Street operation made a conspicuous misstep when meat and alcohol were served at an October 2024 Diwali reception — the first under his Labour government. Conservative MP Shivani Raja formally complained about the "disappointing lack of knowledge of the customs and traditions that many British citizens hold dear." Community organisation Insight UK described it as an "appalling lack of understanding" of Diwali's spiritual significance. Downing Street apologised and promised it would not happen again.

Why Starmer Fell

Starmer's departure was the product of a cascading series of political crises. After winning a historic landslide in July 2024, his administration was battered by plummeting approval ratings, the Peter Mandelson-Jeffrey Epstein scandal, policy reversals, and a crippling domestic energy crisis. The breaking point came when Andy Burnham — the former Manchester mayor who had been building an alternative power base — won the Makerfield by-election on June 18 with 55 per cent of the vote, proving his appeal cut across Labour's fractured voter base.

Starmer spent the following Friday speaking individually to cabinet ministers about whether he could survive. By the weekend, he was writing his resignation speech. The defence secretary, John Healey, had already resigned over what he called inadequate military funding — puncturing Starmer's claim that he always got "the big calls right."

Burnham's Arrival and the Road Ahead

Andy Burnham arrived at Buckingham Palace shortly after Starmer's departure audience with the King, becoming Britain's fourth PM in almost four years of Charles's reign. In a deliberate break from precedent, Burnham addressed the nation without a podium — a signal of the informal, plain-speaking style he cultivated as Manchester mayor.

He promised to end rough sleeping as his first act, announced a ten-year plan for national renewal, and pledged cost-of-living support "starting tomorrow" — with reports suggesting energy bill cuts and a return to the £2 bus fare cap. The hospitality sector, which includes a significant number of Indian restaurant owners across Britain, will be watching closely: Burnham has pledged a 20 per cent reduction in business rates for pubs and music venues, and a cut in hospitality VAT from 20 per cent to 10 per cent.

What British Indians Are Watching For

For Britain's 1.8 million-strong Indian-origin community, the transition raises questions about cultural engagement and economic policy. Burnham's track record as Manchester mayor includes strong ties with the city's diverse communities, but his parliamentary record on issues of specific interest to British Indians — from visa policies to trade relations with India — is thinner than Starmer's, who personally negotiated elements of the UK-India free trade agreement during his tenure.

The hospitality industry relief Burnham has promised could be particularly significant for the thousands of Indian restaurant owners who have struggled under rising costs and post-Brexit staffing shortages. Whether the new PM can translate Manchester-style community engagement into national policy remains the central question of his early premiership.
